questions.text: Why must an admitted, descriptor-pinned backend still undergo policy checks for every live call?

options.A: Because a stable descriptor proves the user has current authorization.
options.B: Because admission evidence automatically expires after each request.
options.C: Because registry publication grants access only after discovery succeeds.
options.D: Because current roles, arguments, backend health, and approvals can change independently of admission.

questions.explanation: Admission establishes which backend may be used, not whether this principal may perform this operation now. Runtime policy evaluates current request conditions.

questions.text: A gateway computes tools/list differently for different users. Which caching approach preserves that visibility boundary?

options.A: Use private cache scope and include the authorization context in the cache key.
options.B: Use public cache scope whenever tool names are deterministically sorted.
options.C: Cache one shared list because all backends passed admission.
options.D: Key the list only by the URL and rely on a short TTL.

questions.explanation: Principal-dependent visibility requires private caching scoped to authorization context. Stable sorting and short TTLs do not prevent cross-user reuse.

questions.text: In Gateway.handle, RBAC allows a direct tool call and its rate bucket has capacity, but the live descriptor digest differs from its pin. What happens before _forward?

options.A: The gateway refreshes the pin automatically and forwards the call.
options.B: It forwards because RBAC approval overrides descriptor changes.
options.C: It records pin_mismatch and returns HTTP 409 with error -32010.
options.D: It removes only the list entry and forwards the direct call.

questions.explanation: The call path checks _is_pinned before _forward. A mismatch is audited and returns HTTP 409 with a Descriptor changed JSON-RPC error.
